headline: NZ Parliament Advances Move-on Orders Bill Amid Homelessness and Rights Debate
summary: Parliament gave first-reading support to bills creating police move-on powers and a new legal framework for disability support, with both measures drawing sharp criticism over rights, consultation and the treatment of vulnerable people. MPs also debated cuts to housing assistance and public-service jobs, while the Government defended withholding updated cost estimates for a major Northland highway project. The move-on bill’s proposed select-committee timetable remained unresolved when the House adjourned.

topicSummaries.topic: Move-on Orders Bill Passes First Reading Amid Homelessness Dispute
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposal could require people, including rough sleepers and those begging, to leave public areas for up to 24 hours, with prosecution possible for refusing to comply.
topicSummaries.content: Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith said the bill would give police a tool to address low-level disorder, intimidation and obstruction in public places, and argued it would help protect businesses and people using city centres. The proposed orders could apply to people aged 14 and over and include rough sleeping and begging among the listed behaviours; lawful protest and charitable fundraising would be exempt. Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori argued the measure would punish people without homes and raised concerns about potential fines, imprisonment and rights to movement and expression. ACT and New Zealand First backed the bill, citing public safety and police discretion. It passed its first reading 67-55 and was referred to the Justice Committee. Debate over the Government’s proposed 3 September report-back date, and amendments seeking more time or fewer committee powers, was interrupted and will resume at the next sitting.

keyExchanges.speaker: Paul Goldsmith (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The Government has no policy to criminalise homelessness. What we do have is a policy to give the police the power to issue move-on orders to people displaying disorderly behaviour in public places, and only people who refuse to follow those orders will face prosecution.

keyExchanges.speaker: Tamatha Paul (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: The Minister realises they don’t have a home, right? Where exactly are they supposed to move on to?

topicSummaries.topic: Disability Support Services Bill Advances Despite Rights and Consultation Concerns
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill would establish rules for publicly funded disability support and could affect family carers’ employment claims and how future support decisions are made.
topicSummaries.content: Disability Issues Minister Louise Upston said the bill would provide a legal framework for Disability Support Services, clarify the use of funding and improve consistency and transparency; she said it would not change current eligibility or introduce means testing. The bill also seeks to limit historical employment claims by paid family carers following a Supreme Court ruling that two carers were Crown employees, while the Minister said the two successful claims and subsequent remedies would not be affected. Labour supported creating a framework but opposed the bill as drafted, raising concerns about ministerial powers, secondary legislation and the extinguishing of unresolved claims. The Greens and Te Pāti Māori opposed it, citing inadequate consultation and possible effects on disabled people’s rights and family carers. National, ACT and New Zealand First supported the bill, which passed its first reading 67-55 and was referred to the Social Services and Community Committee, with a report-back deadline of 13 August.

keyExchanges.speaker: Louise Upston (National)
keyExchanges.quote: To be clear, this bill does not change current eligibility and access to support, nor does it introduce any new requirements for disabled people, families, and carers.

keyExchanges.speaker: Priyanca Radhakrishnan (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: If that’s what the Minister holds on to, it is her responsibility to clarify that in the primary legislation, not the secondary legislation.

topicSummaries.topic: 6,400 Families Face Average $42 Weekly Accommodation Supplement Cut
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The change is expected to reduce housing assistance for thousands of families with children, including some low- and middle-income homeowners.
topicSummaries.content: Social Development Minister Louise Upston said the Government had raised the accommodation supplement entry threshold for homeowners to focus assistance on people it considers most in need, particularly renters. She estimated 9,300 clients would be affected, including 6,400 families with children, whose average entitlement would fall by $42 a week. Green MP Ricardo Menéndez March challenged the change, citing ministry concerns about increased housing insecurity and financial stress and asking whether affected households could face reductions of up to $59 a week. Upston acknowledged that conditions were challenging but argued homeowners had greater choices than renters and said the changes would allow more support to go to renters.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ricardo Menéndez March (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: What does she say to the families who, according to her own ministry, could experience “increased risk of housing insecurity and financial stress”?

keyExchanges.speaker: Louise Upston (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I’ve acknowledged that times are challenging at the moment, and what we must do as a Government is ensure that we are targeting the support to those who have greater needs.

topicSummaries.topic: Public Agencies Face 4% Role Reductions as Government Targets $2.4B Savings
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed reductions could affect public services and employment in communities across New Zealand, not just Wellington.
topicSummaries.content: Public Service Minister Paul Goldsmith said all public agencies were expected to reduce their roles by 4%, with larger agencies accounting for more of the cuts. He set an in-principle target of a public-service workforce below 55,000 by mid-2029 and said the Government expected to save $2.4 billion over the Budget period through workforce changes, restructuring and digitisation. Labour MP Camilla Belich questioned whether a cost-benefit analysis supported the workforce target and asked how the Government could be confident of savings before agency mergers were settled. Goldsmith said many affected roles were outside Wellington and defended the changes as a way to improve value and performance.

keyExchanges.speaker: Camilla Belich (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Is there a cost-benefit analysis underpinning the 55,000 fulltime-equivalent cap for public servants, and if not, why not?

keyExchanges.speaker: Paul Goldsmith (National)
keyExchanges.quote: I haven’t seen that particular analysis, just as I didn’t see any analysis about increasing the size of the Public Service by 18,000, which the previous administration undertook, but I’m pretty sure—I don’t know; I could be wrong—that that costs a lot more.

topicSummaries.topic: Warkworth–Te Hana Road Cost Estimate Remains Withheld During Procurement
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The project’s last published estimate was up to $3.8 billion, and the eventual cost will affect taxpayers and transport investment decisions.
topicSummaries.content: Green MP Julie Anne Genter pressed Transport Minister Chris Bishop to disclose the latest estimate and benefit-cost ratio for the Warkworth to Te Hana road. Bishop confirmed the last public estimate was $2.9 billion to $3.8 billion, but said updated figures were being refined during design and procurement and would be released after a commercial contract was finalised. He argued disclosure could weaken the Crown’s negotiating position. Genter questioned the project’s value, while Bishop defended it on safety, reliability, resilience and economic-connection grounds. The Ombudsman had, according to Bishop, formed the view that the information could be withheld during commercial negotiations.

keyExchanges.speaker: Julie Anne Genter (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: Does the Minister really believe that the Warkworth to Te Hana expressway is the best use of multi-billions of public money, when that route will carry less than 0.1 percent of daily motor vehicle trips, and if so why?

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Bishop (National)
keyExchanges.quote: It is not just about vehicle movements; it’s about safety and reliability and resilience.

topicSummaries.topic: Government and Labour Clash Over Declined Specialist Referrals
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Whether patients are being turned away from specialist care affects access to diagnosis and treatment across the health system.
topicSummaries.content: Labour’s Ayesha Verrall questioned why data supplied to the Association of Salaried Medical Specialists showed more referrals being declined in seven districts. Associate Health Minister Casey Costello, answering for the Health Minister, said Health New Zealand reported that the proportion declined had fallen over the past year, and that the specialist-assessment waiting list had dropped by more than 4,500 since January 2025. Costello said referrals were clinically triaged and patients whose referrals were declined continued to be managed by their family doctor. Verrall asked for the Government’s latest data and questioned whether staffing controls were limiting access; Costello said the data would be made available and that assessments and elective treatment volumes were now ahead of plan.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ayesha Verrall (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Will the Minister release that latest data that she claims shows a different result from the increasing number of declined referrals in the data released to the Association of Salaried Medical Specialists (ASMS)?

keyExchanges.speaker: Casey Costello (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The data that I have quoted today, I’m sure, will be made available to the member.

conclusion: The Government secured first-reading support for two contested bills, but the day’s debates left unresolved concerns about homelessness, disability rights, household support and the scrutiny of major policy decisions.
